new.title: Tour the Bauhaus Dessau building by Gropius
new.desc: Walter Gropius designed this glass-walled school building in 1925-26 as the home of the Bauhaus after its move from Weimar. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and still houses a design school. Workshop wing, aula and the Prellerhaus student studios can be visited on tours.
new.tip: Guided tours run daily and are worth booking in summer; a café and shop sit in the building. Dessau station is a 15-minute walk.

new.title: See the Masters' Houses of Gropius and Kandinsky
new.desc: Gropius built a row of modernist villas in a pine grove in 1925-26 for Bauhaus masters including Kandinsky, Klee, Moholy-Nagy and Feininger. Some were destroyed in WWII; the Kandinsky/Klee and Feininger houses have been restored and the Gropius house was rebuilt as a reconstruction.
new.tip: Interiors are open as a museum; combine with the Bauhaus building on foot along Ebertallee. Check opening days, as winter hours are shorter.

new.title: Walk the Bauhaus Törten housing estate
new.desc: Gropius planned this estate of 314 terraced houses from 1926 to 1928 as an experiment in affordable, industrially built housing. The Konsumgebäude and the Stahlhaus were part of it, and a Törten house with original fittings is open to visitors.
new.tip: Wander the Peterholzstraße area on foot; the visitor house is open on set days. It is a short tram or bus ride south of the centre.

new.title: Visit Schloss Wörlitz, Germany's first Neoclassical palace
new.desc: Prince Leopold III Friedrich Franz of Anhalt-Dessau had Friedrich Wilhelm von Erdmannsdorff build this palace from 1769 to 1773, the first Neoclassical country house in Germany. It stands at the heart of the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and keeps its original interiors and art collection.
new.tip: Entry is by timed tours in the season; the palace is closed in winter, so check dates. Park access is free.

new.title: Find Schloss Luisium, the prince's gift to Luise
new.desc: Prince Franz built this small Neoclassical palace in 1774-78 for his wife Luise, again to designs by Erdmannsdorff. It sits in a landscape park with a Gothic dairy and a Temple and is part of the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm UNESCO site.
new.tip: The palace is open for tours in the season; the park is quiet and good for an unhurried walk. Reach it by bike from Dessau.

new.title: Explore Schloss Georgium and its Gemäldegalerie
new.desc: This Neoclassical palace built from 1780 to 1787 by Erdmannsdorff for Prince Johann Georg holds the Anhalt Picture Gallery with works by Lucas Cranach and Dutch masters. It lies within the Georgium landscape park, part of the Garden Realm.
new.tip: The picture gallery is indoors and suits a rainy day. Check seasonal opening days; the park is free.

new.title: Admire Merseburg Cathedral and its famous charms
new.desc: The cathedral of St John and St Laurence was founded in 1015 and rebuilt over the centuries into a mix of Romanesque and Gothic. Its library holds the Merseburg Charms, among the oldest German-language pagan texts, written in the 9th or 10th century. The cathedral also has the tomb of King Rudolf of Swabia.
new.tip: The cathedral is open daily with a fee for the treasury and museum. Pair it with the castle next door.

new.title: See the Renaissance Schloss Merseburg and its ravens
new.desc: The four-winged palace beside the cathedral was built in its present form from the 15th to 17th century and was the residence of the dukes of Sachsen-Merseburg. It houses the cultural history museum, and legend tells of a raven that stole a ring, kept in a cage in the courtyard.
new.tip: The courtyard is free; the museum charges admission. Walk down to the baroque palace garden afterwards.

new.title: Step into Goethe's theatre at Bad Lauchstädt
new.desc: Goethe built this theatre in 1802 for the Weimar court company, which played here each summer in the spa town. It survives almost unchanged, with a simple wooden auditorium, and stages performances today. The Kurpark and spa buildings stand just beside it.
new.tip: Tours run most days; evening performances are worth booking ahead. Combine it with a walk in the Kurpark.
new.q: Goethe-Theater Bad Lauchstädt, Parkstraße 18, Bad Lauchstädt

new.title: Climb to Burg Wettin, ancestral seat of the Wettins
new.desc: This hill castle above the Saale is the cradle of the House of Wettin, which later ruled Saxony, Poland and the British royal family by marriage. The site goes back to Carolingian times, and today the lower and upper castle are partly used as an art academy and for events.
new.tip: The castle is on the Saale cycle path; the views from the ridge over the valley are best in clear weather. Check access to the upper castle in advance.

new.title: Reach Petersberg's Romanesque priory church
new.desc: The Petersberg is a hill north of Halle crowned by the Romanesque Klosterkirche of the Lauterberg priory, once the Wettin family's burial place. It is a stop on the Romanesque Road and gives wide views over the Saale plain.
new.tip: The church is open on set days and for services; a viewing walk around the hill is free all year.

new.title: Explore Burg Querfurt, one of Germany's largest castles
new.desc: Burg Querfurt covers some 3 hectares and is among the biggest castle complexes in Germany. It has a Romanesque collegiate church from 1140, a medieval dungeon-like Bergfried and a museum with a lapidarium. Its history goes back to the 9th century.
new.tip: Open daily in season with a longer break in winter; allow two hours. The castle also hosts medieval markets.

new.title: Visit Luther's birth house in Lutherstadt Eisleben
new.desc: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483 and this house is the traditional birthplace. It is part of the UNESCO site Luther Memorials, with a museum showing the family home and the reformer's early life. It was restored after a fire in 1689.
new.tip: Combine the ticket with the death house nearby; allow an hour. Open year-round, closed Mondays in winter.

new.title: See Luther's death house at Andreaskirchplatz
new.desc: Martin Luther died in Eisleben on 18 February 1546 in a house on Andreaskirchplatz, now a museum within the UNESCO Luther Memorials. It displays a death mask, a plaster cast and items on the reformer's last days, including the Eisleben text of his last sermon.
new.tip: Visit together with the St Andreas church next door, which has Luther's pulpit. Tickets are shared with the birth house.

new.title: Walk the walls of Schloss Mansfeld
new.desc: The Mansfeld counts' castle high above the town was Luther's childhood setting, as his father worked in the nearby mines. The complex combines Romanesque, Gothic and Renaissance parts and has views over the Wipper valley.
new.tip: Check opening times, as the castle is run by a foundation and often used for events. Cars can park near the gate.

new.title: Smell 8,700 varieties at the Europa-Rosarium
new.desc: Founded in 1903, the Europa-Rosarium in Sangerhausen holds the world's largest rose collection, with around 8,700 species and varieties laid out in a 12-hectare park. The peak bloom is typically in June and July.
new.tip: Open daily; bring a bike or use the small train. A visit in late June catches the roses at their best.

new.title: Stroll the half-timbered lanes of Stolberg
new.desc: Stolberg, in a narrow valley on the southern edge of the Harz, is known as the 'Gold Mine of the Harz', and is packed with more than 300 half-timbered houses. Thomas Müntzer was born here, and the castle sits above the Markt.
new.tip: Park at the edge and walk the main street; the castle has a small museum. A good half-day with lunch.

new.title: Climb the Josephskreuz tower above Stolberg
new.desc: The Josephskreuz is a 38 metre lattice tower built in 1834 on the Auerberg to a design by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, with a cross shape. It is the highest point of the southern Harz area, with views of the Kyffhäuser and Thuringian basin.
new.tip: Open most days in season for a small fee; the steps are steep. Hiking trails lead up from Stolberg.

new.title: Visit the medieval convent of Kloster Helfta
new.desc: Founded in 1258, Helfta was home to the mystics Mechthild of Magdeburg, Gertrud the Great and Mechthild of Hackeborn. It was refounded as a Cistercian convent in 1999 and is a stop on the Romanesque Road, with a church, garden and guesthouse.
new.tip: Open to visitors daily; quiet respect expected during services. It lies on the edge of Eisleben.
new.q: Kloster St. Marien zu Helfta, Lindenstraße 36, Lutherstadt Eisleben

new.title: Lunch at Kornhaus Dessau on the Elbe terrace
new.desc: The Kornhaus is a Bauhaus building from 1929-30 by Carl Fieger on the Elbe embankment, designed as a restaurant and dance hall. It was carefully restored in 2012 and serves regional dishes in rooms with original details.
new.tip: Sit on the Elbe terrace in summer; try a regional lunch dish such as roast with potatoes. Reserve for weekend evenings.

new.title: Have coffee and cake at Café Hilde by the Bauhaus Museum
new.desc: Café Hilde is on Mies-van-der-Rohe-Platz next to the Bauhaus Museum Dessau, a light, modern café that serves coffee, cakes and light lunches.
new.tip: Order a slice of the daily cake and coffee after the museum; check weekday opening times.

new.title: Try Baumkuchen at Konditorei Mrosek in Dessau
new.desc: Mrosek is a long-running confectioner with cafés in Dessau, listing Baumkuchen, the layered cake associated with Saxony-Anhalt, among its pastries.
new.tip: Buy a slice of Baumkuchen and a coffee; there are two branches, Askanische Straße and Kavalierstraße.

new.title: Dine at the historic inn Zum Eichenkranz in Wörlitz
new.desc: Zum Eichenkranz is a historic inn at the entrance to Wörlitzer Park, originally a guesthouse built under Prince Leopold III of Anhalt-Dessau in the 18th century. It has a small beer garden and a restaurant.
new.tip: Try the regional dishes and homemade cakes after the park walk; the beer garden is the draw in summer.

new.title: Linger at Café Ben Zi Bena under Merseburg's cathedral
new.desc: This café and restaurant stands on Domplatz in the middle of the old town between the cathedral and castle, with outdoor tables and a cosy interior, serving lunch and coffee.
new.tip: Take a seat outside on the square in summer; opening hours are typically around 11:00 to 17:00, so go in the afternoon.
new.q: Café Ben Zi Bena, Domplatz 6, Merseburg

new.title: Buy homemade cake at Café und Backhaus Rahaus in Merseburg
new.desc: Café und Backhaus Rahaus on Hallesche Straße is a local bakery with a café, noted for its coffee and homemade cakes.
new.tip: Come for the cake and a coffee; it is a good stop between the station and the old town.
new.q: Café und Backhaus Rahaus, Hallesche Straße 86, Merseburg

new.title: Eat fish at Pier 5 on the Geiseltalsee marina
new.desc: Pier 5 is the restaurant at the Marina Mücheln harbor on the Geiseltalsee, a former lignite pit flooded in the 2000s and now Germany's largest artificial lake by volume. It serves German and Mediterranean dishes with lake views.
new.tip: Reserve a terrace table at sunset; order the fish of the day. Check winter opening days.

new.title: Take coffee at the Burgcafé inside Burg Querfurt
new.desc: The Burgcafé sits within the grounds of Burg Querfurt and serves coffee and cake to visitors of the castle complex.
new.tip: Hours follow the castle; ask at the ticket desk. It is a pleasant stop between museum and church.

new.title: Eat cake in the RosenCafé at the Europa-Rosarium
new.desc: The RosenCafé is the garden café of the Europa-Rosarium in Sangerhausen, surrounded by roses and serving homemade cakes and light meals.
new.tip: Sit outside among the beds in June or July; cakes are made in-house.

new.title: Dine at the Ratsstube on Eisleben's market square
new.desc: The Ratsstube sits on Markt 12 in Lutherstadt Eisleben, close to Luther's statue and the town hall, serving German home cooking in a traditional room.
new.tip: Try a hearty regional main dish; reserve at weekends.

new.title: Book Gaststätte Fischer 'Zum Osterberg' near the Salzige See
new.desc: Gaststätte Fischer in Dederstedt in the Seegebiet Mansfelder Land is a rustic village inn known for its friendly host and honest country cooking, so popular that walk-in visits rarely work.
new.tip: Reserve in advance and ask for the daily special; it is a short drive from Eisleben.

new.title: Tour the Heimkehle, Germany's largest gypsum cave
new.desc: The Heimkehle near Uftrungen in the Südharz is a karst cave system formed in gypsum, with a lake and a large cave hall used for concerts. The cave, visitor centre and exhibition were handed over after a renovation, and guided tours run through the year.
new.tip: Wear warm clothes, as the cave is cool year-round. Check tour times on the cave site.

new.title: Go underground in the Röhrigschacht mine
new.desc: The Röhrigschacht in Wettelrode near Sangerhausen is a copper-shale mine that closed in 1990 and now hosts the largest show mine in Saxony-Anhalt. Visitors descend to the old workings to see the mining techniques of the Mansfeld copper trade.
new.tip: The show mine is closed to visitors from 9 to 26 November 2026 for maintenance and reopens afterwards. Wear sturdy shoes.

new.title: Ride the Mansfelder Bergwerksbahn narrow-gauge train
new.desc: The Mansfelder Bergwerksbahn runs historic narrow-gauge steam and diesel trains on the former copper-mine railway, starting at Klostermansfeld station in Benndorf. It holds themed rides such as the Walpurgis train on 30 April.
new.tip: Trains depart from the historic station at Hauptstraße 15; the timetable runs on set weekends, so check the schedule.

new.title: Swim at the Geiseltalsee beach
new.desc: The Geiseltalsee is a flooded former lignite pit southwest of Halle, now the largest man-made lake in Germany by volume, with beaches and a marina. Free swimming is possible at the Stöbnitz beach on the lake's east side.
new.tip: Swim from June to September; the lake is freely accessible all year round. Bring your own towel and check water signs.

new.title: Walk and swim at the Süßer See near Seeburg
new.desc: The Süßer See in the Mansfelder Land is a natural freshwater lake east of Eisleben, under nature protection. A circular route of around 17 km links Seeburg and the shore, with a viewpoint on Seeburg Castle.
new.tip: Swimming is allowed only at marked spots, such as a gravel beach on the north shore; check signs and water quality first.
new.q: Süßer See, Seeburg, Seegebiet Mansfelder Land

new.title: Glide through Wörlitzer Park by gondola
new.desc: Prince Franz brought gondolas from Venice to the Wörlitz lake, and boat trips on the lakes and canals of the Garden Realm continue the tradition. The ride passes the Gothic House, Rousseau island and the palace.
new.tip: Boats run in season; buy tickets at the jetty. Early morning is quietest.

new.title: Breathe the brine at the Bad Dürrenberg Gradierwerk
new.desc: The Gradierwerk in Bad Dürrenberg is a wooden brine graduation house, described by ADAC as the longest continuous one in Germany, with 12 m high towers in the Kurpark. The brine has been used for health since 1846.
new.tip: Walk the length of the towers and breathe the salt air; the Kurpark was part of the 2024 Landesgartenschau and is free.

new.title: Cross the Saale on the Wettin ferry for a castle view
new.desc: The Saale ferry at Wettin crosses the river near Burg Wettin and is on the Saale cycle path. The crossing gives the best view of the castle and the steep banks.
new.tip: Cross on the ferry, then walk or ride the bank; check the ferry's operating season.

new.title: Hike the Wettin loop to the Bismarck tower
new.desc: A circular hike from the ferry car park climbs through the Saale valley to the Bismarckturm and Burg Wettin, with wide views over the river and the Brachwitz hills.
new.tip: Allow 2 to 3 hours; start at the ferry car park and wear good shoes.

new.title: Stroll Merseburg's baroque Schlossgarten above the Saale
new.desc: The palace garden below Schloss Merseburg was laid out in the baroque style with an orangery annex that has housed a restaurant since 1968. It runs down to the Saale and offers views of the cathedral.
new.tip: The garden is free; guided tours run on set dates. Spring and early summer are best.

new.title: Climb the Hohe Linde spoil heap at Wettelrode
new.desc: The Hohe Linde is a conical mining spoil heap at Wettelrode, left from the copper-shale mining. Guided climbs are held on set days and give long views over the Südharz foothills.
new.tip: The climb is offered on event days; check the Röhrigschacht calendar. Wear sturdy shoes.

new.title: Take a boat tour from the Geiseltalsee marina
new.desc: Boat tours run from Marina Mücheln across the Geiseltalsee, the flooded lignite pit, showing the new shoreline and the former mining landscape.
new.tip: Tours run in season; ask at the Hafenkontor harbour office for dates.
